title: The Rusty Secret of Mars

topics.value_lesson: Patience: the rover goes slowly and carefully, and that is exactly why it discovers things a rushing machine would miss

spine: A little rover follows clues across the red planet to discover why Mars glows red like an ember.

segments.text:
"Look what just came in," says Dr. Maya. She turns her screen toward you, and there it is — a brand-new picture from Mars.

The whole planet glows red. Not gray like the Moon. Not blue like Neptune. Red, like the last ember in a campfire.

"Every night, the other planets send pictures too," Dr. Maya says. "Gray rocks. Blue ice. But Mars?" She taps the screen. "Mars is red all over. The ground, the hills, even the sky is pinkish. And nobody has ever taken a picture that shows us why."

Far away on that red world, a little rover is waking up. His name is Rusty. He has six wheels, one long neck, and two camera eyes that swivel like an owl's.

Rusty looks left. Red dust. He looks right. Red rocks. He looks down at his own wheels — red! He is coated in the stuff, and it never washes off, because it never rains on Mars.

"Trundle, trundle," go his wheels across the rusty plain, and a speck of red dust lifts off the ground and rides the wind beside him.

Today, Dr. Maya has a job for Rusty. "Take a picture," she says, "that tells us the rusty secret of Mars."

Rusty's camera eyes blink. Where does a little rover even begin?

"The tracks," you say. Dr. Maya grins. "Tracks it is."

Trundle, trundle. Rusty rolls to the rim of Thumbprint Crater, and there they are — wheel tracks, pressed into the red dust long, long ago.

"Another rover made these," Dr. Maya says softly. "It stopped working before you were built."

Rusty follows the tracks down, down, down, and the speck of red dust rides the wind after him. At the bottom sits the old rover, still and dusty, its camera eyes closed.

But its last pictures are still inside. Rusty plugs in a cable — click — and the pictures fly home to Earth.

Dr. Maya looks at the first one. Then the next. Her eyes go wide.

"These pictures are years and years old," she says. "Before the big dust storm. Before everything." She turns the screen toward you. "And look — the ground is red in every single one."

You lean in close. Red ground. Red rocks. Red, red, red.

"So the dust storm didn't make Mars red," you say.

"No," says Dr. Maya. "Mars was already red. The rusty secret is older than we thought."

The little speck of dust settles on the old rover's back, and stays.

"The volcano," you say. Dr. Maya whistles. "Olympus Mons. The biggest volcano anybody knows."

Trundle, trundle. Rusty climbs the long, gentle slope — so gentle it takes all morning — and the speck of red dust rides the wind beside him, up and up.

At last, Rusty's camera eyes blink at something new. Dark rock, ropy and swirled, like thick porridge poured out and frozen mid-plop.

"Lava," Dr. Maya breathes. "It flowed here once, hot as soup on the stove. Now it's stone. Take the picture, Rusty."

Rusty lifts his long neck. Click.

But the picture comes back red. The lava rock is dark — the picture shows it red!

"Something's on your lens," Dr. Maya says. Rusty swivels one camera eye and looks at the other. There it is: one tiny speck of red dust, stuck to the glass. He wipes it with his little brush. Click again.

Now the rock is dark and true.

Dr. Maya taps her chin. "The dust isn't just on the ground. It floats in the air. It lands on everything — even a camera."

You look at the first red picture, then the clean dark one.

"Is that the secret?" you ask. "Is Mars red because the dust is everywhere?"

"Maybe," says Dr. Maya. "Maybe." And the little speck of dust rides the wind away, looking for somewhere new to settle.

"Come and see," says Dr. Maya. She lays the new picture on the table, right beside the ones from before. "What did you two find out there?"

You tell her. All of it.

She listens. She nods. Then she reaches into her desk drawer and pulls out something small and ordinary — an old nail, the kind you might find in a garden shed. It is not shiny. It is not gray. It is red.

"Watch," she says.

She holds the rusty nail up to the screen, right next to the red dust of Mars. You lean in close.

They are the same color. Exactly the same.

"The nail is made of iron," says Dr. Maya. "When iron sits out in the air long enough, it rusts — and rust is red." Her eyes go wide and bright. "And Mars is covered in iron. Every rock. Every hill. The whole planet rusted, long, long ago."

The rusty secret of Mars.

Far away, a little rover's camera eyes blink. The speck of red dust settles softly on his shoulder, like it has heard the answer too, and is glad somebody finally said it out loud.

"Then let's wait," you say. "Let's see what story the storm leaves."

Far away on Mars, the wind begins to blow. It starts as a whisper, then a whoosh, then a great rumbling tumble of red dust that swallows Rusty whole. The sky turns orange. The sun shrinks to a pale coin, then vanishes completely.

Rusty does not panic. Rusty hunkers down. He tucks his camera eyes close, folds his solar wings, and waits, quiet as a stone. The dust storm whirls around him for one day, two days, three.

Then, slowly, the wind grows tired. The sky opens like a curtain. The pale coin of sun comes back, and Rusty shakes himself — dust flying off in red puffs.

"Look at his panels," Dr. Maya says, pointing. The dust has settled in swirls and stripes, like the lines in a fingerprint. "The wind painted a map on him. It shows us exactly where the storm blew."

You lean in. The red dust on Rusty's back tells the story of the whole storm, written in rust.

"Even the storm carries the secret," Dr. Maya says softly. "It's all the same red."

And far away, a little rover lifts his camera eyes to the sky, and takes a picture of the sun coming back.

"Then let's look here," you say. "Let's find something on Earth that wears the same red."

You turn from the screen, and there — on the windowsill, small as your smallest fingernail — sits a ladybug. Red shell. Dark dots. She has been there the whole time, quiet as a secret.

"Look," you whisper.

Dr. Maya looks. She smiles, and picks up the picture of Mars — the red dust, the red hills, the whole rusty planet — and holds it right beside the windowsill.

You lean in close.

They are almost the same red. Not exactly — the ladybug is brighter, shinier, alive — but close enough to make you gasp. Mars, the biggest red thing you know, and a ladybug, the smallest, wearing nearly matching coats.

"Rust is red," Dr. Maya says softly. "And so is she."

The ladybug opens her wings — one tiny flick — and flies away into the garden. But Dr. Maya does not put the picture down. She pins it to the wall, right beside a photo of a ladybug she took last summer.

"There," she says. "Now the secret has a friend."

Far away, Rusty's camera eyes blink. He turns them around — all the way around — and takes a picture of himself, the red plain stretching behind him like a great rusty blanket. A selfie.

Something small and red to take home.
